slides.heading: One plan, two hopes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **Cabinet Mission** of **1946**, its **clauses**, and why it **failed**.

slides.narration: After the Second World War, Britain was ready to hand over power, but Indian leaders disagreed about what kind of country should follow. In nineteen forty-six three British ministers came to find a plan both major parties could accept. In this part we study the clauses of their plan, and why it could not be carried out.

slides.narration: This timeline shows the eighteen months that ended British rule. The Mission arrived in March nineteen forty-six and announced its plan in May. Direct Action Day came in August, and the interim government in September. In nineteen forty-seven came Attlee's statement in February, the Mountbatten Plan in June, the Act in July and independence in August.

slides.heading: The Cabinet Mission
slides.body_md: Three British **cabinet ministers** came to settle the **constitutional question**.

slides.narration: The Mission had three members: Lord Pethick-Lawrence, who was the Secretary of State for India, Sir Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander. They reached India in March nineteen forty-six, held long talks with leaders of the Congress and the Muslim League, and announced their own plan on the sixteenth of May.

slides.narration: The plan proposed three levels. At the top, a Union of India, including the princely states, would deal with only three subjects: defence, foreign affairs and communications. In the middle, provinces could form groups. At the base, provinces kept all other subjects and the residuary powers, and the states kept everything they did not give to the Union.

slides.heading: Sections A, B and C
slides.body_md: Provinces placed in **three sections**.

rows: Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, Central Provinces, Orissa

visual.alt: Table of the three sections of the 1946 plan: Section A, Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, Central Provinces, Orissa; Section B, Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sind; Section C, Bengal and Assam
visual.caption: Grouping as commonly taught.

slides.narration: The provinces were placed in three sections. Section A held the Hindu-majority provinces such as Madras, Bombay and the United Provinces. Section B held the north-western provinces: Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province and Sind. Section C held Bengal and Assam. Provinces in a section could work together as a group with its own legislature.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: placing provinces
slides.body_md: Place **Sind**, **Assam** and **Orissa** in their sections, with a reason.
bullets: **Sind:** Section **B**, with Punjab and the North-West Frontier Province.
**Assam:** Section **C**, with Bengal.
**Orissa:** Section **A**, with the other Hindu-majority provinces.
Tip: learn **B** and **C** first; everything else is in **A**.

slides.narration: Let us practise. Sind belongs to Section B, together with Punjab and the North-West Frontier Province. Assam belongs to Section C with Bengal. Orissa belongs to Section A with the other Hindu-majority provinces. A simple trick: learn the two small sections, B and C, and remember that every other province was in A.

slides.heading: Making the constitution
slides.body_md: A **Constituent Assembly** elected by the **provincial assemblies**.

visual.alt: Table of the Constituent Assembly under the 1946 plan: 292 seats for the provinces of British India, 4 for the Chief Commissioners' provinces and 93 for the princely states, 389 in all
visual.caption: Seats in the provinces were shared among communities roughly by population.

slides.narration: A Constituent Assembly would frame the constitution. Its members from the provinces were to be elected by the provincial assemblies, not directly by the people, and seats were shared among the General, Muslim and Sikh communities roughly by population. The princely states would also send members. As commonly taught, the Assembly was to have three hundred and eighty-nine seats.

slides.heading: Other clauses
slides.body_md: An **interim government**; **no separate Pakistan**; states free to **negotiate**.

slides.narration: Three more clauses complete the picture. An interim government of Indian leaders would run the country while the constitution was made. The demand for a fully separate Pakistan was not accepted; the groups were offered instead. And the princely states would keep their powers and negotiate their entry into the Union.

slides.heading: The interim government
slides.body_md: Took office on **2 September 1946**, headed by **Jawaharlal Nehru**.

rows: Jawaharlal Nehru (Vice-President of the Executive Council)
First met 9 December 1946; the League stayed away

visual.alt: Table about the interim government: took office 2 September 1946, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru as Vice-President of the Executive Council; the Muslim League joined in October 1946; the Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946 and the League stayed away

slides.narration: The interim government took office on the second of September nineteen forty-six, with Jawaharlal Nehru at its head as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council. The Muslim League joined it in October. The Constituent Assembly first met on the ninth of December, but the League stayed away from it.

slides.heading: Why the plan failed
slides.body_md: Different **readings**, **withdrawal**, **violence** and **distrust**.

nodes.label: Both parties give a qualified acceptance (June 1946)
They read the grouping clauses differently
Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) and violence
Distrust in the interim government; League stays out of the Assembly

visual.alt: Flow of why the 1946 plan failed: both parties give a qualified acceptance in June 1946; they read the grouping clauses differently; the League withdraws its acceptance in July; Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946 is followed by violence; distrust grows in the interim government and the League stays out of the Assembly
visual.caption: From acceptance to deadlock.

slides.narration: At first both parties accepted the plan, each with its own reading of the grouping clauses. Disputes over whether grouping was compulsory led the League to withdraw its acceptance in July and to call for Direct Action Day on the sixteenth of August. Violence followed in Calcutta and other places, and people of every community suffered. Distrust then made the plan unworkable.

slides.narration: To sum up Part One. The Cabinet Mission arrived in March nineteen forty-six and, on the sixteenth of May, proposed one Union with only three subjects, groups of provinces in three sections, a Constituent Assembly and an interim government. Both parties accepted it at first, but different readings, the League's withdrawal, Direct Action Day and the violence that followed made it unworkable.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Plan announced **16 May 1946**.
Union: **defence, foreign affairs, communications** only.
Section B = **Punjab, NWFP, Sind**; Section C = **Bengal, Assam**.
Assembly elected by **provincial assemblies**, not directly.
Describe the **violence** of 1946 **humanely**, without blaming any community.

slides.narration: On the twentieth of February nineteen forty-seven the British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, announced that Britain would transfer power to Indian hands by June nineteen forty-eight at the latest. Lord Mountbatten replaced Lord Wavell as Viceroy in March, with the task of arranging the transfer.

slides.heading: The plan of 3 June 1947
slides.body_md: Two **dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**.

slides.narration: On the third of June nineteen forty-seven Mountbatten announced his plan. The country was to be split into two dominions, called India and Pakistan. Areas would choose between them in different ways, a boundary commission would mark the borders, the princely states could join either dominion, and power would pass much earlier than planned, on the fifteenth of August.

slides.heading: How Punjab and Bengal decided
slides.body_md: Assemblies voted in **two parts**.

slides.narration: Punjab and Bengal each had Muslim-majority districts and districts where others were in a majority. So the members of each assembly met in two parts and voted separately. If either part voted to divide the province, it would be divided, and a boundary commission would mark the line between the two new parts.

The princely states, freed from British control, could join either dominion. In the end each of these areas chose its dominion before or soon after independence.

slides.heading: Why the plan was accepted
slides.body_md: Accepted **reluctantly**, as the **lesser evil**.

visual.caption: Present the reasons neutrally; critics' concerns are noted in the notes.

slides.narration: Why did Congress leaders accept a plan that divided the country? Violence was spreading and they feared civil war. The interim government could not work as a team. The plan offered an early transfer of power, in August nineteen forty-seven, and a strong central government for the rest of India. Many accepted it reluctantly, as the lesser of two evils.

slides.heading: Two views of 1947
columns:
**Supporters said**

- It ended a **deadlock** and gave an **early** transfer of power.
- It allowed a **strong centre** for the rest of India.

**Critics said**

- It **divided provinces** and families.
- It went against the idea of a **united, secular** India.

visual.alt: Comparison table: the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 proposed one Union with groups, did not accept Pakistan, kept Punjab and Bengal whole in Sections B and C, and asked states to join the Union by negotiation; the Mountbatten Plan of 1947 created two dominions, accepted Pakistan, allowed Punjab and Bengal to be divided by vote, and let states join either dominion
visual.caption: Two plans, two answers to the same question.

slides.narration: Present both views fairly. Supporters said the plan ended the deadlock, brought freedom early and allowed a strong central government. Critics said it divided provinces and families, led to great suffering, and went against the idea of one united, secular India for which the national movement had worked. A good answer gives both sides.

slides.heading: Two plans compared
slides.body_md: **One Union** in 1946; **two dominions** in 1947.

rows: Kept whole in Sections B and C

visual.alt: Comparison table: the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 proposed one Union with groups, did not accept Pakistan, kept Punjab and Bengal whole in Sections B and C, and asked states to join the Union by negotiation; the Mountbatten Plan of 1947 created two dominions, accepted Pakistan, allowed Punjab and Bengal to be divided by vote, and let states join either dominion
visual.caption: Two plans, two answers to the same question.

slides.narration: Compare the two plans. The Cabinet Mission Plan of nineteen forty-six tried to keep one Union, with groups of provinces, and did not accept Pakistan. The Mountbatten Plan of nineteen forty-seven accepted two dominions and allowed Punjab and Bengal to be divided. The change shows how far the situation had moved in one year.

slides.heading: The Indian Independence Act, 1947
slides.body_md: Royal assent on **18 July 1947**; in force from **15 August 1947**.

visual.caption: Paraphrased; no text of the Act is reproduced.

slides.narration: The British Parliament turned the plan into law through the Indian Independence Act, which received the royal assent on the eighteenth of July nineteen forty-seven. From the fifteenth of August two independent dominions came into being. Each Constituent Assembly would make its constitution and also act as its legislature, and the Government of India Act of nineteen thirty-five would apply meanwhile.

slides.heading: More clauses of the Act
slides.body_md: **Paramountcy** lapses; the **Secretary of State** goes; London loses power.

slides.narration: The Act made other changes. British paramountcy over the princely states lapsed, so they had to decide their future. The Secretary of State for India, the minister in London, lost his office. Each dominion had a Governor-General acting on the advice of its own cabinet. And the British Parliament could no longer make laws for India.

The Congress accepted it as the lesser evil. The Independence Act made it law, and India became free on the fifteenth of August.

sections.heading: 2. Constituent Assembly, states and interim government
sections.body_md:
- **Constituent Assembly:** members from the provinces **elected by the provincial assemblies** by proportional representation, seats shared among the **General, Muslim and Sikh** communities roughly by population; the **princely states** also represented (389 seats, as commonly taught).
- **Princely states** to keep all subjects not ceded to the Union and to **negotiate** their entry.
- **Interim government** of Indian leaders while the constitution was framed; it took office on **2 September 1946**, headed by **Jawaharlal Nehru**; the League joined in **October 1946**.
- The **Constituent Assembly** first met on **9 December 1946**; the League stayed away.

sections.heading: 3. Why the plan could not be carried out
sections.body_md:
- Both major parties gave a **qualified acceptance** in **June 1946**, but **read the grouping clauses differently** (compulsory or optional).
- The **Muslim League** withdrew its acceptance in **July 1946** and called for **Direct Action Day** on **16 August 1946**.
- **Violence** broke out in **Calcutta** and spread to other places; people of **every community** suffered greatly.
- **Distrust** in the interim government and the League's absence from the Assembly made the plan unworkable.

sections.heading: 4. Attlee's statement and the Mountbatten Plan
sections.body_md:
- **20 February 1947:** **Attlee** announced that Britain would transfer power by **June 1948**; **Mountbatten** replaced **Wavell** as Viceroy in **March 1947**.
- **3 June 1947 — clauses (paraphrased):** two **dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**; **Punjab and Bengal** assemblies to vote in **two parts** on dividing the province; a **boundary commission** (headed by **Sir Cyril Radcliffe**) to mark the borders; **Sind** to decide by its assembly; **referendums** in the **NWFP** and **Sylhet**; **princely states** free to join either dominion; power to pass on **15 August 1947**.

key_terms.definition_md: A self-governing country within the British Commonwealth, free to make its own laws.

sections.heading: 5. Why the Congress accepted the plan
sections.body_md:
- **Spreading violence** and fear of **civil war**.
- **Deadlock** in the interim government: ministers of the two parties could not work as a team.
- An **early transfer** of power, in **August 1947** instead of 1948.
- A **strong central government** for the rest of India, without the weak Union of 1946.
- Many leaders saw partition as the **lesser evil** and accepted it **reluctantly**.
- **Critics** felt it divided provinces and families, caused great suffering and went against the idea of a **united, secular** India. Give both views.

key_terms.definition_md: The idea that partition, though painful, was better than continued violence and deadlock.

sections.heading: 6. The Indian Independence Act, 1947
sections.body_md:
- Passed by the **British Parliament**; **royal assent** on **18 July 1947**; in force from **15 August 1947**.
- **Clauses (paraphrased):** two independent **dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**; each **Constituent Assembly** to frame a constitution and act as the **legislature**; the **Government of India Act, 1935**, as adapted, to govern meanwhile; a **Governor-General** for each dominion on the advice of its own cabinet (one person could serve both if they agreed); **British paramountcy** over the states to **lapse**; the office of **Secretary of State for India** abolished; the **British Parliament** to have no power to legislate for the dominions.
- Violence and mass migration accompanied Partition; very large numbers of people were displaced or killed, and estimates vary widely.

key_terms.definition_md: The supreme authority of the British Crown over the princely states, which lapsed on 15 August 1947.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up the **Cabinet Mission** (1946, one Union) and the **Mountbatten Plan** (1947, two dominions).
- Putting **Punjab** in Section **C** (it was in **B**).
- Saying the Constituent Assembly was **directly** elected (it was elected by **provincial assemblies**).
- Saying **Bengal** held a referendum (only the **NWFP** and **Sylhet** did).
- Saying India became a **republic** in 1947 (it became a **dominion**; a republic in **1950**).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct clauses or reasons.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clause or reason per mark; write in your own words.

questions.stem_md: Which three British cabinet members made up the Cabinet Mission that reached India in March 1946?

options.text_md: Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander. The Mission was Lord Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State for India), Sir Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander. Attlee was Prime Minister; Mountbatten came as Viceroy in 1947; Simon led the commission of 1927.

questions.stem_md: On which date was the Cabinet Mission's plan for India's constitutional future announced?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 16 May 1946. The plan was announced on 16 May 1946. 3 June 1947 is the Mountbatten Plan, 16 August 1946 the Direct Action Day and 20 February 1947 Attlee's statement.

questions.stem_md: An imagined official in 1946 sorts government work into piles for the proposed Union of India and for the provinces. Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, which pile belongs to the Union?

options.text_md: Land revenue, police and local government
All subjects, leaving nothing to the provinces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Defence, foreign affairs and communications. The Union was to deal only with defence, foreign affairs and communications, with power to raise the finances these needed. All other subjects and residuary powers stayed with the provinces.

questions.stem_md: An imagined provincial minister in 1946 asks which level of government would control a new matter not named in any list, such as a tax on cinema shows. Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, where would this residuary power lie?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** With the provinces. Residuary powers were to remain with the provinces, keeping the Union weak and limited to three subjects. This was meant to reassure provinces that feared a strong centre.

questions.stem_md: Which provinces formed Section B in the Cabinet Mission's grouping scheme?

options.text_md: Madras, Bombay and the United Provinces
Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province and Sind
Bihar, Orissa and the Central Provinces

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province and Sind. Section B was the north-western provinces: Punjab, the NWFP and Sind. Bengal and Assam formed Section C; Madras, Bombay, UP, Bihar, CP and Orissa formed Section A.

questions.stem_md: What did the Cabinet Mission Plan propose about the demand for a separate, fully sovereign Pakistan?

options.text_md: It did not accept it and proposed a single Union with groups of provinces instead
It accepted it and drew the boundary at once
It left the question to the princely states
It asked the United Nations to decide

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It did not accept it and proposed a single Union with groups of provinces instead. The Mission rejected a fully sovereign Pakistan and offered a loose Union with groups of provinces as a compromise. The boundary of partition came only with the 1947 plan and the boundary commission.

questions.stem_md: How were the members from the British Indian provinces to be chosen for the Constituent Assembly under the Cabinet Mission Plan?

options.text_md: By direct election by all adult citizens
By the rulers of the princely states
By the elected provincial legislative assemblies, seats being shared among communities by population

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** By the elected provincial legislative assemblies, seats being shared among communities by population. Provincial assemblies were to elect the members by proportional representation, with seats divided among the General, Muslim and Sikh communities roughly by population. There was no direct adult-franchise election.

questions.stem_md: The imagined ruler of a small princely state reads the 1946 plan with his adviser. What does the plan allow his state to do?

options.text_md: They would be abolished and merged with provinces at once
They would keep all subjects not handed to the Union and could negotiate their entry
They would come under the direct rule of the British Parliament
They would form Section C of the scheme

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They would keep all subjects not handed to the Union and could negotiate their entry. The states were to keep every subject and power not ceded to the Union, and to negotiate their place in it. They were not abolished, and Section C was Bengal and Assam.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student sorts provinces for a class chart on the 1946 plan. Into which Section should she place Assam?

options.text_md: Section A, with Madras and Bombay
Section B, with Punjab and Sind
No Section, because Assam was a princely state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Section C, together with Bengal. Assam was grouped with Bengal in Section C. Section A held the Hindu-majority provinces, Section B the north-western provinces, and Assam was a province, not a princely state.

questions.stem_md: On which day did the Muslim League observe Direct Action Day after withdrawing its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission Plan?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 16 August 1946. Direct Action Day was 16 August 1946. 15 August 1947 is Independence Day, 9 December 1946 the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly and 2 September 1946 the start of the interim government.

questions.stem_md: When was the interim government proposed by the Cabinet Mission sworn in, with Jawaharlal Nehru at its head?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** September 1946. The interim government took office on 2 September 1946, with Nehru as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council. The Muslim League joined it in October 1946.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined debate on the 1946 plan, a speaker says a province placed in a group should be able to leave it later. Which provision of the plan supports this speaker?

options.text_md: A province could leave the Union at any time by a vote of its governor
Provinces had no choice once grouped
Only princely states could change groups
A province could opt out of its group after the first general election under the new constitution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A province could opt out of its group after the first general election under the new constitution. The plan allowed a province to come out of its group after the first general elections under the new constitution. Provinces could not leave the Union at will, and the provision was about provinces, not states.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Cabinet Mission Plan gave the Union of India only three subjects.

**Reason (R):** The Mission wanted to reassure provinces that feared a strong central government while keeping India united.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: a weak Union with only defence, foreign affairs and communications was the compromise meant to keep the country together without a strong centre.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the Cabinet Mission Plan the Constituent Assembly was to be elected directly by all adult Indians.

**Reason (R):** The plan provided for an interim government of Indian leaders while the constitution was being made.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the provincial assemblies, not the voters directly, were to elect the members. R is true: an interim government of Indian leaders was part of the plan.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Cabinet Mission Plan proposed that the Union of India would include both British India and the princely states.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Union was to embrace both British India and the princely states, dealing with defence, foreign affairs and communications.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Muslim League called for Direct Action Day while it still accepted the Cabinet Mission Plan.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The League first accepted the plan, then withdrew its acceptance in July 1946 and called for Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946.

questions.stem_md: The Cabinet Mission Plan grouped the provinces into ___ sections, named A, B and C.
questions.solution_md: There were three sections: A (Hindu-majority provinces), B (the north-west) and C (Bengal and Assam).

questions.stem_md: Match each province with the Section of the 1946 grouping scheme in which it was placed.

match_right.text_md: Section A, with the other Hindu-majority provinces

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Bombay and Orissa were in Section A, Sind in Section B (north-west), and Bengal in Section C with Assam.

questions.stem_md: State any two clauses of the Cabinet Mission Plan about the structure of the Union.
questions.solution_md: Any two structural clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **Union of India** of British India and the **princely states**, handling **defence, foreign affairs and communications**.
2. **Residuary** and all other powers with the **provinces**, which could form **groups** (Sections A, B and C).

questions.stem_md: Give two provisions of the 1946 plan about the body that would frame India's constitution.
questions.solution_md: Election by assemblies; seats by community and population; states represented.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **Constituent Assembly** whose provincial members were **elected by the provincial assemblies** by proportional representation.
2. Seats shared among the **General, Muslim and Sikh** communities by population, with **princely states** also represented.

questions.stem_md: An imagined newspaper of 3 September 1946 reports that Indian leaders have just taken charge of the government departments. Identify this body and say when it took office.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and date.

answer.model_answer_md: It was a government of **Indian leaders** holding the portfolios of the Viceroy's **Executive Council** while the constitution was framed. It took office on **2 September 1946**, headed by **Jawaharlal Nehru**.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the Muslim League's response to the Cabinet Mission Plan changed between June and August 1946.
questions.solution_md: Acceptance, withdrawal, Direct Action Day.

answer.model_answer_md: The League first **accepted** the plan in **June 1946**, but after disputes over its meaning it **withdrew** its acceptance in **July** and called for **Direct Action Day** on **16 August 1946**, which was followed by **serious violence**.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Cabinet Mission propose grouping the provinces into Sections A, B and C?
questions.solution_md: Reassure Muslim-majority provinces; keep one Union.

answer.model_answer_md: Grouping let the **Muslim-majority** provinces of the north-west and east act together on many subjects, meeting some of the League's concerns, while keeping a **single Union** and so **avoiding partition**.

questions.stem_md: Describe three clauses of the Cabinet Mission Plan other than those about the Constituent Assembly.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Union of India** of British India and the states, for **defence, foreign affairs and communications**.
2. **Groups:** provinces placed in **Sections A, B and C**, free to form groups with their own executives and legislatures.
3. **Interim government** of Indian leaders, and **rejection** of a fully sovereign **Pakistan**.

questions.stem_md: Why did the Cabinet Mission Plan, accepted at first by both major parties, fail to settle the future of India? Give three reasons.
questions.solution_md: Differing interpretations; withdrawal and violence; distrust.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The parties **read the grouping clauses differently**: one saw grouping as **compulsory**, the other as **optional**.
2. The League **withdrew its acceptance** in **July 1946** and called **Direct Action Day**, after which **violence** spread.
3. Distrust deepened in the **interim government**, so the plan's idea of **one Union** could not be carried out.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Cabinet Mission of 1946.

(i) Who were the members of the Cabinet Mission, and when did it announce its plan? **[3]**
(ii) State three clauses of the plan about the Union and the provinces. **[3]**
(iii) State four clauses of the plan about the Constituent Assembly, the princely states and the interim government. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Members and date; Union and provinces; Assembly, states, interim government.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Mission was **Lord Pethick-Lawrence**, the Secretary of State for India, **Sir Stafford Cripps** and **A. V. Alexander**. It reached India in **March 1946** and announced its plan on **16 May 1946**.

(ii) A **Union of India** of British India and the **princely states** would handle **defence, foreign affairs and communications**. All other subjects and **residuary powers** would stay with the **provinces**. The provinces were placed in **three sections (A, B, C)** and could form **groups**.

(iii) A **Constituent Assembly** would be elected by the **provincial assemblies**, seats being shared by **community and population**. The **princely states** would also send members and would keep all subjects not given to the Union. An **interim government** of Indian leaders would run the country meanwhile. A fully sovereign **Pakistan** was **not accepted**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the period after the Cabinet Mission Plan.

(i) How did the two major parties respond to the plan at first? **[3]**
(ii) Why did the Muslim League withdraw its acceptance, and what did it call for? **[3]**
(iii) Explain how the events of August–December 1946 made the plan harder to carry out. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Responses; withdrawal and Direct Action; violence, distrust and boycott.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Both parties gave a **qualified acceptance**. The **Muslim League** accepted the plan in **June 1946**, seeing the groups as a step towards its aims. The **Congress** accepted the plan for the **Constituent Assembly**, but with its own reading of the **grouping** clauses.

(ii) After statements suggesting the Assembly would not be bound by the grouping scheme, the League feared its interests would not be protected. In **July 1946** it **withdrew** its acceptance and called for **Direct Action Day** on **16 August 1946**.

(iii) **Violence** broke out in **Calcutta** and spread to other places, causing great suffering to people of **all communities**. The **interim government** took office in **September** without the League, which joined only in **October** amid distrust. The League **boycotted** the **Constituent Assembly** when it met on **9 December 1946**, so the idea of one agreed Union faded.

questions.stem_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The top tier was the **Union of India**, which would include both **British India** and the **princely states**. It was given only three subjects: **defence**, **foreign affairs** and **communications**, with the power to raise the money needed for them.

(ii) **Section B** grouped the north-western provinces: **Punjab**, the **North-West Frontier Province** and **Sind**. **Section C** grouped the eastern provinces of **Bengal** and **Assam**. Both sections had Muslim majorities or large Muslim populations.

(iii) For the **Congress**, the scheme kept **one Union** of the whole country, **rejected partition**, and gave India a single **Constituent Assembly** to frame its constitution. For the **League**, the **weak centre** with only three subjects, the **residuary powers** left with the provinces, and the right of Muslim-majority provinces to act together in **groups** with their own legislatures offered **protection** that came close to its demand, without dividing the country.

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from the imagined diary of a junior clerk in Delhi and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The Cabinet Mission Plan.

**(b)** Section B.

**(c) (i)** Interim government; purpose.

**OR (c) (ii)** League boycott.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **Cabinet Mission Plan** of **16 May 1946**.

**(b)** **Section B** (Punjab, the NWFP and Sind).

**(c) (i)** The **interim government** headed by **Jawaharlal Nehru**, which took office on **2 September 1946**. The plan provided for Indian leaders to run the government **while the constitution was being framed**.

**OR (c) (ii)** The **Muslim League** had withdrawn its acceptance of the plan and **boycotted** the **Constituent Assembly**, so its elected members did not attend the **first meeting**.

questions.passage_md:
**Diary of an imagined clerk in a government office, New Delhi, 1946**

17 May. Everyone in the office is reading the newspapers about the plan of the three visiting ministers. The centre will look after only the army, foreign affairs and the posts and railways; the rest stays with the provinces. My colleague from Lahore says his province will sit with Sind and the Frontier. 3 September. A new Indian council has taken charge of the departments today. 9 December. The assembly that will write the constitution held its first meeting, but many benches were empty.

children.stem_md: Which plan is the clerk reading about on 17 May?

answer.model_answer_md: The **Cabinet Mission Plan** of **16 May 1946**.

children.stem_md: In which Section of the plan would the colleague's province "sit with Sind and the Frontier"?

answer.model_answer_md: **Section B** (Punjab, the NWFP and Sind).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): What was the "new Indian council" of 3 September, and why was it formed?

answer.model_answer_md: The **interim government** headed by **Jawaharlal Nehru**, which took office on **2 September 1946**. The plan provided for Indian leaders to run the government **while the constitution was being framed**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Why might "many benches" have been empty at the meeting of 9 December 1946?

answer.model_answer_md: The **Muslim League** had withdrawn its acceptance of the plan and **boycotted** the **Constituent Assembly**, so its elected members did not attend the **first meeting**.

questions.stem_md: In February 1947, by which date did the British Prime Minister say power would be transferred to Indian hands?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** June 1948. Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947 set June 1948 as the latest date. Power was in fact transferred earlier, on 15 August 1947.

questions.stem_md: On which date was the plan of Lord Mountbatten for the transfer of power announced?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 3 June 1947. The Mountbatten Plan was announced on 3 June 1947. 16 May 1946 is the Cabinet Mission Plan, 18 July 1947 the royal assent to the Independence Act and 20 February 1947 Attlee's statement.

questions.stem_md: How was the question of dividing Punjab and Bengal to be decided under the 3 June plan?

options.text_md: Members of each provincial assembly would meet in two parts, by Muslim-majority and other districts, and vote
A referendum of all adults in India would decide

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Members of each provincial assembly would meet in two parts, by Muslim-majority and other districts, and vote. Each assembly was to meet in two parts, representing the Muslim-majority districts and the rest; if either part voted for partition, the province would be divided. No all-India referendum was held.

questions.stem_md: In which two areas did the 3 June 1947 plan provide for a referendum to decide which dominion they would join?

options.text_md: The North-West Frontier Province and the Sylhet district of Assam

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The North-West Frontier Province and the Sylhet district of Assam. Referendums were held in the NWFP and in Sylhet. Punjab and Bengal decided through their assemblies; Sind through its assembly; princely states such as Hyderabad and Kashmir were left to choose.

questions.stem_md: After the Punjab assembly votes for division in June 1947, an imagined district officer asks who will decide which villages go to which dominion. What does the 3 June plan provide?

options.text_md: A boundary commission to mark the new borders
An election commission for the princely states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A boundary commission to mark the new borders. A boundary commission was to demarcate the border within Punjab and Bengal; it was headed by Sir Cyril Radcliffe. The other bodies played no part in drawing the boundary.

questions.stem_md: In July 1947 the imagined dewan of a princely state asks what choice the plan announced in June leaves his ruler. What is the answer?

options.text_md: They would stay under British rule
They could join either India or Pakistan

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They could join either India or Pakistan. With British paramountcy ending, the princely states were free to join either dominion. In practice they were advised to join the one to which they were geographically linked.

questions.stem_md: An imagined teacher in Shillong in July 1947 tells her class that people in one district of their province will vote on which country to join. Which district is she describing?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Sylhet. Sylhet, a Muslim-majority district of Assam, decided by referendum. Lahore was in Punjab, Dacca in Bengal and Peshawar in the NWFP, which held its own referendum but is not in Assam.

questions.stem_md: Which reason best explains why many Congress leaders agreed to the partition plan of 1947?

options.text_md: They believed partition would be reversed within a year
The princely states had demanded partition
Widespread communal violence and a deadlocked interim government made an early, agreed transfer seem the lesser evil
The British had refused to leave India without it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Widespread communal violence and a deadlocked interim government made an early, agreed transfer seem the lesser evil. Leaders accepted partition reluctantly because violence was spreading and the interim government could not work as a team, so an early, agreed transfer of power seemed better than continued conflict. The other options are not supported.

questions.stem_md: An imagined news-sheet of June 1947 reports that the date for handing over power has been brought forward. To which date was it brought forward?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 15 August 1947. The transfer was advanced from June 1948 to 15 August 1947. 26 January 1950 is when the Constitution came into force.

questions.stem_md: In what form was power to be transferred under the 3 June plan?

options.text_md: To two dominions, India and Pakistan
To one federation including all princely states
To the United Nations for a period of trust

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** To two dominions, India and Pakistan. Power was to pass to two dominions, India and Pakistan, each with its own Constituent Assembly. The other options do not describe the plan.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the 3 June plan the Punjab and Bengal assemblies met in two parts to vote on partition.

**Reason (R):** Each of these provinces had Muslim-majority districts and districts where others were in a majority.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: because each province had districts of both kinds, its assembly was split into two parts so that each could decide whether to divide the province.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The transfer of power was advanced from June 1948 to August 1947.

**Reason (R):** Lord Mountbatten replaced Lord Wavell as Viceroy in March 1947.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The date was advanced because of the worsening situation and the need for an early settlement; the change of Viceroy is a separate fact.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The 3 June plan provided for a referendum of all the people of Bengal on partition.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. In Bengal and Punjab the decision lay with the assembly members voting in two parts; referendums were held only in the NWFP and Sylhet.

questions.stem_md: Lord ___ was the Viceroy who announced the plan of 3 June 1947 for the transfer of power.
questions.solution_md: Lord Mountbatten, who became Viceroy in March 1947, announced the plan; it is named after him.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these events of 1946–47 in the order in which they happened.

options.text_md: The Cabinet Mission Plan is announced
Attlee announces the British will leave by June 1948

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). May 1946 plan, August 1946 Direct Action Day, February 1947 Attlee's statement, June 1947 Mountbatten Plan.

questions.stem_md: State any two clauses of the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947.
questions.solution_md: Any two clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. British India would be **divided** into two **dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**.
2. The **Punjab and Bengal** assemblies would meet in **two parts** and vote on **partitioning** their provinces.

questions.stem_md: What did the British Prime Minister announce on 20 February 1947, and why was it important?
questions.solution_md: Announcement and importance.

answer.model_answer_md: He announced that Britain would **transfer power** to Indian hands by **June 1948**. It made the British **departure certain** and pressed Indian parties to reach a **settlement** quickly.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the Congress accepted the plan of 3 June 1947.
questions.solution_md: Any two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Communal violence** was spreading and leaders feared **civil war**.
2. The **interim government** could not work as a team, so an **early, agreed transfer** of power seemed the lesser evil.

questions.stem_md: How were the futures of the North-West Frontier Province and the Sylhet district to be settled under the 1947 plan?
questions.solution_md: Referendum; outcomes.

answer.model_answer_md: Both were to decide by a **referendum** of their people. The **NWFP** voted to join **Pakistan**, and **Sylhet**, a district of **Assam**, also voted to join **Pakistan**.

questions.stem_md: Describe three clauses of the Mountbatten Plan about how areas would choose between India and Pakistan.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Punjab and Bengal:** assembly members of Muslim-majority districts and of the others would vote **separately**; a vote for division by either part would **partition** the province.
2. **Sind** would decide through its assembly; the **NWFP** and **Sylhet** through **referendums**.
3. **Princely states** were free to join **either dominion**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the plan of 3 June 1947.

(i) What had the British Prime Minister announced in February 1947, and who became Viceroy soon after? **[3]**
(ii) State three clauses of the Mountbatten Plan. **[3]**
(iii) Give four reasons why the Congress accepted the plan. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Background; clauses; reasons for acceptance.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) On **20 February 1947** **Attlee** announced that Britain would **transfer power** by **June 1948**. Soon after, in **March 1947**, **Lord Mountbatten** took over from **Lord Wavell** as the new Viceroy.

(ii) British India would be divided into **two dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**. The **Punjab and Bengal** assemblies would vote in **two parts** on **partition**, and a **boundary commission** would mark the borders. **Referendums** would be held in the **NWFP** and **Sylhet**, and **princely states** could join **either** dominion.

(iii) **Communal violence** was spreading, and leaders feared **civil war**. The **interim government** could not function as a team. An **early transfer** of power, on **15 August 1947**, would end British rule quickly. Many leaders saw partition as the **lesser evil** that would leave a strong, united India in the rest of the country.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the decisions of 1947.

(i) Explain how the plan of 3 June 1947 differed from the Cabinet Mission Plan on the unity of India. **[3]**
(ii) Explain the role of the boundary commission. **[3]**
(iii) "Partition was accepted as the lesser of two evils." Give two arguments that support this view and two concerns raised by its critics. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Contrast; boundary commission; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **Cabinet Mission Plan** proposed **one Union** with groups of provinces and **rejected** a separate Pakistan. The **3 June plan** accepted **partition** into **two dominions**, with Punjab and Bengal also divided if their assemblies so voted.

(ii) Once **Punjab** and **Bengal** chose division, a **boundary commission** headed by **Sir Cyril Radcliffe** was to mark the new **borders** between the dominions, district by district, on the basis of **contiguous majority areas** and other factors.

(iii) **Support:** it offered an **early, peaceful transfer** of power when violence was spreading; and it ended the **deadlock** in the interim government, allowing a **strong central government** in India. **Concerns:** it **divided provinces** and families and led to **mass migration** and **suffering**; and many felt it went against the idea of a **united, secular** India for which the national movement had worked.

questions.stem_md: Read the extract from an imagined letter and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined document written by SOYL for practice; the people in it are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** The Mountbatten Plan.

**(b)** Boundary commission.

**(c) (i)** Violence; deadlock and early freedom.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two parts; either votes for division.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **Mountbatten Plan** of **3 June 1947**.

**(b)** The **boundary commission** (headed by **Radcliffe**) that would mark the new border in **Punjab**.

**(c) (i)** To **end the fighting**, that is the **communal violence**; and to end the **quarrels in Delhi**, meaning the **deadlock** in the **interim government**, so that freedom could come **early**.

**OR (c) (ii)** The **Punjab assembly** would meet in **two parts**, members from **Muslim-majority districts** and the **rest**. If **either part** voted for division, the province would be **partitioned**.

**Letter from an imagined schoolteacher in Amritsar to her brother in Bombay, June 1947**

Brother, the radio has given the news we feared. The country will become two, and our own province may be cut in two as well: the members of our assembly will sit in two groups and vote. The leaders say it is better to end the fighting and the quarrels in Delhi and take freedom now than to wait another year. I am not sure what to think.

children.stem_md: Which plan of June 1947 is the "news we feared" in the letter?

answer.model_answer_md: The **Mountbatten Plan** of **3 June 1947**.

children.stem_md: What is the "commission" that will "draw the line through the villages"?

answer.model_answer_md: The **boundary commission** (headed by **Radcliffe**) that would mark the new border in **Punjab**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Which two reasons for accepting the plan does the letter mention?

answer.model_answer_md: To **end the fighting**, that is the **communal violence**; and to end the **quarrels in Delhi**, meaning the **deadlock** in the **interim government**, so that freedom could come **early**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain the procedure by which "our own province may be cut in two".
alternatives.solution_md: Two parts; either votes for division.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Punjab assembly** would meet in **two parts**, members from **Muslim-majority districts** and the **rest**. If **either part** voted for division, the province would be **partitioned**.

questions.stem_md: In which month of 1947 did the Indian Independence Act, passed by the British Parliament, receive the royal assent?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** July. The Act received the royal assent on 18 July 1947 and took effect on 15 August 1947. The plan it put into law had been announced in June.

questions.stem_md: On 15 August 1947 an imagined student writes in her diary what the new law from London has just created. Which entry is correct according to the Indian Independence Act?

options.text_md: A single federation of India and the states
Two independent dominions, India and Pakistan
An Indian republic with an elected President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Two independent dominions, India and Pakistan. Two independent dominions came into being on 15 August 1947. India became a republic only on 26 January 1950.

questions.stem_md: What did the Indian Independence Act provide about British paramountcy over the princely states?

options.text_md: It would lapse, ending British authority over them
It would pass to the Government of India
It would pass to the Government of Pakistan

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It would lapse, ending British authority over them. Paramountcy lapsed on 15 August 1947; it was not transferred to either dominion. The states then decided on accession.

questions.stem_md: Which British office concerned with India was abolished by the Indian Independence Act?

options.text_md: The Secretary of State for India
The Speaker of the House of Commons

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Secretary of State for India. The office of the Secretary of State for India was abolished. Each dominion kept a Governor-General, and the British offices of Prime Minister and Speaker were not affected.

questions.stem_md: In late 1947 an imagined journalist notices that the body writing India's constitution is also passing ordinary laws. Which provision of the Indian Independence Act explains this?

options.text_md: It could only advise the Governor-General
It could only choose the Prime Minister
It could frame the constitution and also act as the dominion's legislature
It had no power until the British Parliament approved its laws

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It could frame the constitution and also act as the dominion's legislature. Each Constituent Assembly was to frame a constitution and also act as the legislature, with full power to make laws. The British Parliament lost its authority over the dominions.

questions.stem_md: An imagined official in Delhi in September 1947 needs to know which law still governs the working of the new government until India's own constitution is ready. What should she consult?

options.text_md: The Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted. Until new constitutions were made, each dominion was governed by the Government of India Act, 1935, with necessary changes. The plan of 1946 was not a law, and the Constitution came only in 1950.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student says that after 15 August 1947 the head of state of each new dominion was a Governor-General. Which provision of the Act is she describing?

options.text_md: The British Prime Minister would govern both dominions
The Secretary of State for India would remain head of both
The President of the Constituent Assembly would be head of state
Each dominion would have a Governor-General appointed by the Crown on the advice of its own cabinet

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Each dominion would have a Governor-General appointed by the Crown on the advice of its own cabinet. The Act provided a Governor-General for each dominion, appointed on the advice of that dominion's cabinet. The Secretary of State's office was abolished.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Indian Independence Act seen as ending Britain's legal authority over India?

options.text_md: It made the British monarch the President of India
It placed India under the League of Nations
After 15 August 1947 no law of the British Parliament would apply to the dominions unless they adopted it
It kept the Secretary of State in charge of foreign affairs

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** After 15 August 1947 no law of the British Parliament would apply to the dominions unless they adopted it. From the appointed day, the British Parliament could no longer legislate for the dominions, and their own legislatures became sovereign. The other options are wrong.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After 15 August 1947 the princely states had to decide their future relationship with the dominions.

**Reason (R):** The Indian Independence Act provided that British paramountcy over the states would lapse.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: with paramountcy lapsing, the states were no longer tied to the British Crown and had to choose accession to India or Pakistan.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Indian Independence Act came into force on 15 August 1947.

**Reason (R):** The Act made India a republic on the same day.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true. R is false: India became a dominion on 15 August 1947 and a republic only on 26 January 1950.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Indian Independence Act allowed the same person to be Governor-General of both dominions if they so agreed.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The Act permitted a common Governor-General if both dominions wished; in practice India and Pakistan had separate Governors-General.

questions.stem_md: The Indian Independence Act fixed ___ August 1947 as the day on which the two dominions came into being.
questions.solution_md: The appointed day was 15 August 1947.

questions.stem_md: State any two clauses of the Indian Independence Act, 1947.
questions.solution_md: Any two clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. From **15 August 1947** two independent **dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**, would come into being.
2. **British paramountcy** over the **princely states** would **lapse**.

questions.stem_md: What two roles did the Indian Independence Act give the Constituent Assembly of India?
questions.solution_md: Constitution-making; legislature.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. To **frame the constitution** of the dominion.
2. To act as its **legislature** (Parliament), with **full power** to make laws, until the new constitution came into force.

questions.stem_md: An imagined clerk in a London ministry learns in August 1947 that his department is closing. Name the office that ended under the Indian Independence Act, and the office that would head each new dominion.
questions.solution_md: Abolished office; kept office.

answer.model_answer_md: The office of the **Secretary of State for India** was **abolished**. Each dominion would have a **Governor-General**, appointed on the advice of its own **cabinet**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ruler of a small princely state asks his adviser in August 1947 whether the British Crown still protects his state. What should the adviser reply, using the Indian Independence Act?
questions.solution_md: Paramountcy lapsed; choice of accession.

answer.model_answer_md: The adviser should say **no**: the Act ended **British paramountcy** on **15 August 1947**, so the state must now decide whether to **join India or Pakistan**.

questions.stem_md: Describe three clauses of the Indian Independence Act other than the creation of two dominions.
questions.solution_md: Three clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **British paramountcy** over the **princely states** would **lapse**.
2. Each **Constituent Assembly** would frame a constitution and act as the **legislature**; until then the **Government of India Act, 1935** would apply as adapted.
3. The office of **Secretary of State for India** would be **abolished**, and each dominion would have a **Governor-General**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the Indian Independence Act, 1947.

(i) When was the Act passed, and from what date did it take effect? **[3]**
(ii) State three clauses of the Act about the dominions and their governments. **[3]**
(iii) State four other clauses of the Act. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Dates; dominions and governments; other clauses.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **British Parliament** passed the Act in **July 1947**, and it received the **royal assent** on **18 July 1947**. It took effect on **15 August 1947**, the appointed day.

(ii) Two independent **dominions**, **India** and **Pakistan**, would come into being. Each would have a **Governor-General** appointed on the advice of its own **cabinet**. The **Constituent Assembly** of each would frame its **constitution** and act as its **legislature**.

(iii) **British paramountcy** over the **princely states** would **lapse**. The office of **Secretary of State for India** would be **abolished**. Until new constitutions were ready, each dominion would be governed by the **Government of India Act, 1935**, as **adapted**. The **British Parliament** would have no power to make laws for the dominions after the appointed day.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following.

(i) How did the Indian Independence Act give legal effect to the plan of 3 June 1947? **[3]**
(ii) Explain what the Act meant for the princely states. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why the Act is seen as the legal end of British rule in India. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Legal effect; states; end of British authority.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **3 June plan** was a political scheme. The Act turned it into **law**: it created the **two dominions**, fixed the appointed day as **15 August 1947**, and provided for the **boundaries** of Punjab and Bengal to be settled by the **boundary commission**.

(ii) The Act ended **British paramountcy**, so the treaties binding the states to the Crown **lapsed**. The states had to decide on their **accession**, and most chose to join **India** or **Pakistan** by signing an **Instrument of Accession**.

(iii) From the appointed day the **British Parliament** could no longer make laws for the dominions. The **Secretary of State for India** disappeared, and power passed to the **Constituent Assemblies** and to **cabinets** responsible to them. The **Governor-General** acted on the advice of Indian ministers, so authority now rested with the **people of India**.

questions.stem_md: In which year did the Cabinet Mission come to India?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1946. The Mission arrived in March 1946 and announced its plan in May 1946. 1942 is the Cripps Mission; 1947 the Mountbatten Plan.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the 1946 grouping scheme, Punjab was placed in Section C.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Punjab was in Section B, with the NWFP and Sind; Section C was Bengal and Assam.

questions.stem_md: Under the 3 June 1947 plan, an assembly met in two parts to vote on dividing its province. Which pair of provinces did this apply to?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Punjab and Bengal. The two-part vote applied to Punjab and Bengal, which had both Muslim-majority and other districts. Sind decided through its whole assembly and the NWFP by referendum.

questions.stem_md: The boundary commission that drew the line in Punjab and Bengal was headed by Sir Cyril ___.
questions.solution_md: Sir Cyril Radcliffe headed the boundary commissions; the award was announced just after independence.

questions.stem_md: Which day did the Indian Independence Act fix as the appointed day for the new dominions?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 15 August 1947. The appointed day was 15 August 1947. 3 June is the plan, 18 July the royal assent and 26 January 1950 the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Indian Independence Act abolished the office of the Secretary of State for India.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. With the end of British authority, the office of the Secretary of State for India was abolished.

questions.stem_md: Who headed the interim government that took office in September 1946?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Jawaharlal Nehru. Jawaharlal Nehru headed the interim government as Vice-President of the Executive Council; Wavell was Viceroy at the time, Mountbatten came in 1947 and Pethick-Lawrence led the Cabinet Mission.

questions.stem_md: Until India's new constitution was ready, which earlier Act was to govern the dominion, with changes?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Government of India Act, 1935. The Government of India Act, 1935, as adapted, served as the provisional constitution. The other Acts belonged to earlier periods.
